title: MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEM CYBERATTACK
executiveAssessment: Publicly available evidence establishes that a coordinated wave of malicious cyber activity targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems on July 26-27, 2026 . Minnesota IT Services (MNIT) publicly announced the incident on July 28, 2026, and stated that the activity affected technology used to remotely monitor and control water-system equipment. MNIT later specified that most confirmed cases involved PLCs and HMIs . MNIT, July 28, 2026 ; MNIT release, July 30, 2026 Public reporting and subsequent federal warnings strongly support that the activity was part of a broader late-July 2026 pattern affecting water and wastewater utilities in multiple U.S. states. On July 30, 2026, the FBI and EPA warned that water and wastewater utilities in at least seven states had reported incidents since July 27, and that some activity had degraded water operations. That PSA identified observed attacker behavior against internet-facing Rockwell Automation / Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs : remote access, changes to IP addresses and passwords , loss of monitoring/control, and in at least one case modified PLC project files with ladder-logic discrepancies. FBI/EPA PSA, July 30, 2026 The publicly defensible conclusion is that the Minnesota incidents were technically consistent with exploitation of internet-exposed OT/PLC environments , potentially including cellular-modem or other remote-access exposure, and that the adversary's actions focused on disrupting operator visibility and control rather than publicly confirmed water contamination or destructive process manipulation. CISA separately warned the same day that attackers were targeting PLCs in the water sector and that this activity included undocumented external connections such as cellular modems installed by operators, vendors, or system integrators . CISA bulletin, July 30, 2026 However, several critical points remain unresolved. Minnesota explicitly stated on July 30, 2026 that it was not attributing the activity to a specific actor , would not release system-specific forensic findings or access details while the investigation remained active, and had not determined that every incident was carried out by the same actor. Public reporting later cited unnamed U.S. officials suggesting likely Iranian involvement, but those reports did not amount to public authoritative attribution by Minnesota, CISA, or the FBI. MNIT release, July 30, 2026 ; Washington Post, July 30, 2026 ; CBS News, updated Aug. 1, 2026 Bottom line: The strongest public evidence supports a coordinated, multi-victim OT intrusion/disruption campaign against Minnesota community water systems during July 26-27, 2026, likely exploiting internet-exposed control environments. Public evidence does not support confirmed attribution, confirmed water contamination, or a complete public victim list.

methodology: Confirmed activity Targets were OT systems used for remote monitoring and control. MNIT release In the FBI/EPA-described pattern, actors remotely accessed internet-facing PLCs . FBI/EPA PSA Observed attacker actions included changing PLC IP addresses and setting/changing passwords , causing loss of monitoring and control. FBI/EPA PSA At least one organization in the multi-state set reported modified PLC project files and ladder-logic discrepancies . FBI/EPA PSA CISA stated threat actors had modified passwords to lock out operators and changed IP addresses to disconnect PLCs. CISA bulletin Assessed activity Assessment Likely initial access path: exposed OT reachable from the internet, potentially directly exposed PLC interfaces or intermediary connectivity such as cellular modems or remote-management paths. This is supported by the FBI/EPA and CISA warnings, but Minnesota did not publicly disclose case-specific access details. FBI/EPA PSA ; CISA bulletin ; MNIT release Unresolved Whether the Minnesota incidents involved default credentials, weak credentials, unauthenticated access, a software vulnerability, or a combination of these mechanisms. Unresolved Whether attackers moved beyond PLC/HMI environments into engineering workstations, historians, or broader IT networks. Unresolved Whether any destructive or stealth persistence mechanism was used. Vulnerabilities, access mechanisms, and products reportedly involved The FBI/EPA PSA identified observed targeting of Rockwell Automation / Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs . FBI/EPA PSA Rockwell issued recovery and hardening guidance, stating there was no CVE associated with its notice and characterizing the issue as threat-actor activity against internet-exposed controllers rather than a vendor vulnerability disclosure. Rockwell advisory index / SD1790 summary Federal and CISA-associated Iran-related guidance before the incident emphasized public internet exposure, default or common passwords, remote-access services, and inadequate segmentation as recurring OT risks. FBI/CISA fact sheet, June 30, 2025 Important analytical control: Public evidence does not support naming a specific exploited CVE, vendor flaw, or credential set in the Minnesota cases. Repeating such claims as fact would exceed available evidence.
impact: Confirmed cyber/operational impact Plymouth experienced a communications outage affecting water facilities and continued operating through manual procedures until communications were restored. Water levels and quality were reported unaffected. City of Plymouth MNIT said "impacted" meant investigators confirmed malicious activity involving a system's technology and explicitly cautioned that not every affected community experienced water-service disruption. MNIT release FBI/EPA reported that in the broader multi-state set, operational effects included loss of pressure and flooding . FBI/EPA PSA CISA stated the broader activity had resulted in boil-water notices and sustained manual operations . CISA bulletin Water-quality and public-safety consequences Confirmed Fact Minnesota publicly stated there were no active requests for residents to modify drinking-water use as of July 30, 2026. MNIT release Confirmed Fact CBS reported a Minnesota DPS spokesperson said none of Minnesota's water supply had been reported compromised as a result of the attack. CBS News Unresolved Whether any Minnesota system experienced pressure loss, flooding, boil-water orders, equipment damage, or direct process disruption specifically due to malicious activity. MNIT said the state was continuing to assess whether specific equipment issues or operational disruptions resulted directly from malicious activity. MNIT release Unresolved Financial recovery costs for Minnesota utilities were not publicly quantified in the reviewed sources.

sections.heading: FINAL ASSESSMENT
sections.text: WHAT DO WE KNOW? A coordinated cyber incident wave targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems on July 26-27, 2026. MNIT Confirmed affected technology included PLCs and HMIs used to remotely monitor and control equipment. MNIT release Broader federal reporting described concurrent multi-state targeting of internet-facing Rockwell MicroLogix PLCs with IP/password changes causing loss of monitoring/control and, in some cases, degraded operations. FBI/EPA PSA Minnesota publicly stated there were no active requests to change drinking-water use and did not publicly confirm contamination or statewide public-health effects. MNIT release WHAT DO WE ASSESS? The Minnesota incidents were likely enabled by a shared OT exposure pattern, most plausibly internet-accessible PLC/remote-access pathways, potentially including cellular modems or integrator-installed connectivity.
